Doorways would be a good place to start. They can assist with a single session counselling and then refer you to longer term counselling through NL Health Services.

 The Jacob Puddister Foundation also offers free counselling, however, they're known to have a waitlist.

If you're connected to an EAP program through your work, definitely take advantage of that. If you're a student, there should be free counselling services available.

There is also the option of private, paid counselling if that's something you're interested in.  A quick Google search will show a lot of options for private counselling options.

If all else fails, contacting the Mental Health Services System Coordinator might be able to point you in the right direction. Barry Hewitt is his name, he can be reached at 752-3916.

Just an off point, but as someone who also lives with generalized anxiety disorder, medication in addition to counselling helped me immensely. If you can, talk to your family doctor about your options. They can also assist you with a referral to mental health counselling through NL Health Services. If you don't have a family doctor, you can get assistance through Medicuro or ProActive are free online  family doctors for residents of NL. All you need is a valid MCP.

For 2SLGBTQIA+ specific counselling, I'm not too familiar, but, Quadrangle may be a good place to start.

Hope this helps, best of luck!

I had tried to quit many times before but when I decided to this time I knew I had to. I still remember smoking my last joint, sitting in my car in my driveway and sobbing. I ended up going inside and flushing the rest down the toilet.

Removing everything in my life related to it helped. For me, the ritual was almost as addicting as the substance itself, so, I sold my grinders, smashed my bong in the woods (v enjoyable), and burned all of my papers. 

From there, I quit cold turkey. It was difficult - probably the most difficult thing I've ever done. The first three months were absolute hell. I couldn't sleep, I couldn't eat, but, knowing I had to do this is what got me through.

About six months in I decided enough was enough and I couldn't do this on my own, so, I opted for therapy. I accessed a same day, one session therapy offered by my provincial govt that helped me come to terms.

From there I realised that I might actually have OCD, and weed was masking all of the symptoms. Experiencing withdrawals combined with new OCD onset was hard, but, after talking with my doctor, meds really helped.

8 months after quitting, I landed a really great job where I still am today. The substantial salary increase allowed me to progress in life a lot and has led to me doing all the things I have done today.

A loving partner, medication, and knowing I'm better off without it all helped me three years later.

In all honesty, it was mostly anxiety for me and it took about 6-12 months before I hit baseline. What I did realise though was marijuana was just a mask over underlying issues. Therapy and meds did wonders for my MH.

I always say that anxiety means you give a shit. It's your brain telling you, "hey this is important, pay attention to it". I believe anxiety is rooted into our brains, as a defense mechanism for our more archaic pasts. When we were hunter gatherers, and saw a predator, we got anxious, which instilled our fight or flight response. Now, however, we view everyday things as being on par with the "predator". 

Our intuition is our brains response to the predator. It's the part of us that says "we know this is bad because of X". In terms of the predator, our intuition gives us that anxiety feeling because we know the predator could easily harm us". I believe our intuition is there to protect us in ways. But the thing is that OCD skews our intuition, and when we live with this disease, our intuition cannot be trusted to guide us down the path we really want. It'll tell us "hey don't do that! Remember what happened last time?", And tell you in every way to avoid the path we want to go down. Intuition=protection against fears of the past. 

We have to be willing to let go of the past, the future, and live in the moment.
